title: A Statistical Theory of Gated Attention through the Lens of Hierarchical Mixture of Experts
claim: Gated attention variants attain faster polynomial estimation rates than standard multi-head attention, shown by steeper log-log loss decay with sample size.
layout: 2x3 grid of log-log plots, rows by K, columns by model
description: A 2x3 grid of log-log line plots. Columns correspond to MHA, Value Gated Attention and SDPA Gated Attention. The top row uses K=3 and the bottom row uses K=4. Each panel plots Voronoi loss (y-axis, log scale) against sample size from 10^4 to 10^5 (x-axis, log scale). Blue lines with dots and vertical error bars show the empirical loss. A dashed orange line shows the fitted power law, and the fit is written in the legend. The MHA fits are shallow, with exponents of about -0.12 and -0.13. The gated attention fits are steeper, at about -0.49 to -0.53. The eye goes first to the noisy blue curves and then to the exponents in the legends. Panel captions such as '(a) MHA (K=3)' sit below each plot.
caption: Log-log plots of empirical Voronoi losses versus sample size n for multi-head self-attention and gated attention mechanisms with Sigmoid activation function (Experiment 1).
abstract: Self-attention has greatly contributed to the success of the widely used Transformer architecture by enabling learning from data with long-range dependencies. In an effort to improve performance, a gated attention model that leverages a gating mechanism within the multi-head self-attention has recently been proposed as a promising alternative. Gated attention has been empirically demonstrated to increase the expressiveness of low-rank mapping in standard attention and even to eliminate the attention sink phenomenon. Despite its efficacy, a clear theoretical understanding of gated attention's benefits remains lacking in the literature. To close this gap, we rigorously show that each entry in a gated attention matrix or a multi-head self-attention matrix can be written as a hierarchical mixture of experts. By recasting learning as an expert estimation problem, we demonstrate that gated attention is more sample-efficient than multi-head self-attention. In particular, while the former needs only a polynomial number of data points to recover the model parameters, the latter requires exponentially many data points to achieve the same estimation error. Furthermore, our analysis also provides a theoretical justification for why gated attention is more effective at mitigating the attention sink phenomenon and the low-rank bottleneck when a gate is placed at the output of the scaled dot product attention or the value map rather than at other positions in the multi-head self-attention architecture.
